name: Annasäule Innsbruck
kurzbeschreibung: The Annasäule on Innsbruck's Maria-Theresien-Straße: erected in 1704–1706 by Cristoforo Benedetti from red Kramsacher Marmor in thanksgiving for the liberation of the land in 1703.
beschreibung:
Overview

The magnificent Annasäule is one of the most famous landmarks of the Tyrolean provincial capital Innsbruck and forms the monumental centerpiece of the prestigious Maria-Theresien-Straße pedestrian zone. Set against the spectacular natural backdrop of the steeply towering limestone peaks of the Nordkette, this Baroque votive column rises as a world-renowned photo subject. Erected at the beginning of the 18th century, the artwork commemorates a dramatic chapter of regional defense and stands as a masterwork of Trentine Baroque sculpture.

History & Artwork

The column's creation traces back to a vow made by the Tyrolean Estates in 1703: during the War of the Spanish Succession, Bavarian troops under Elector Max Emanuel invaded Tyrol to subjugate the territory for France and Bavaria. In a fierce popular uprising, the Tyrolean riflemen succeeded on July 26, 1703 – the Catholic feast day of Saint Anne – in decisively repelling the enemy troops at the Pontlatzer Brücke and at the Brennerpass, freeing the land from the invaders (known as the Bayrische Rummel). Out of deep gratitude for divine deliverance, the Estates commissioned the votive monument. The renowned sculptor Cristoforo Benedetti from Castione near Trent was entrusted with its design and execution. Between 1704 and 1706, the work was created from polished red Kramsacher Marmor. On July 26, 1706, exactly three years after the liberation, the monument was solemnly consecrated by Prince-Bishop Johann Philipp von Lamberg. The Corinthian column is crowned by the statue of the Immaculata (the Immaculate Conception of Mary), watching over the city with a crescent moon and a crown of stars. Flanking the richly articulated pedestal are four artfully crafted statues of saints: Saint Anne as the namesake patron of the vow day, Saint George with the dragon as the patron saint of Tyrol, and the two diocesan patrons Cassian (Brixen) and Vigilius (Trent). In 1958, the weather-sensitive original statues were replaced with faithful replicas; the originals are preserved in the Tyrolean state museum Ferdinandeum.

Visit & Getting There

The Annasäule stands freely accessible in the center of the traffic-calmed pedestrian zone and can be admired year-round at any time of day or night free of charge. Arriving by public transport: From Innsbruck Hauptbahnhof, walk in approx. seven minutes through Salurner Straße or Brixner Straße directly into Maria-Theresien-Straße. Trams and city buses stop at the surrounding stations Anichstraße/Rathausgalerien or Maria-Theresien-Straße. By car: Parking in the central underground garages Rathausgalerien, Kaufhaus Tyrol, or Altstadtgarage.

Tips

The entire pedestrian zone around the Annasäule is paved level and accessible without thresholds for wheelchair users and strollers. The surrounding street cafes and outdoor terraces invite you to enjoy a coffee in summer while admiring the column and the Nordkette massif. The classic photo view succeeds looking from south to north: from here, the statue of Mary is framed picture-perfect by the rock faces of the Inntal range.
